transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Session begins. Each player has Petra 3 FP, Anselm 3 FP, Caddock 3 FP, Yarrow 3 FP. Face-up: Rising Floodwaters [H-03], The Pikemaw [T-05].

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rain hammers the cedar-shingle roofs of Hollowmoot as your punt bumps against the last dry landing before the toll gate. Lantern light gutters on chains strung between pilings, and a knot of soaked, shivering families presses against a Warden barring the causeway north — he's got a torch in one hand and a ledger in the other, and he's not budging. Behind you, the water is already higher than the landing markers from last week, black and restless, swallowing the lower steps of the nearest stilt-house. Somewhere out past the reeds, faint and wrong, you can hear what might be a bell.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: That bell—it's wrong, Coss. It's calling for help, and the water won't wait for your ledger. Please. Let these people through.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra grips the punt pole, her eyes still fixed on that dark water beyond the reeds where the bell-song drifts. Every muscle in her is tense, listening to something the others can't quite hear. She glances at the shivering families pressed against Coss's torch, then back to the Warden—a plea and a warning all at once. She's already reading the water levels, already calculating how much time they have before even the Causeway goes under.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: That bell... I know that sound. It's old liturgy crying from the deep water, and it's calling. I have to reach those reeds.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm pushes past the shivering families toward the railing, his eyes fixed on the dark water beyond the landing where the sound seems to pulse from the reeds. For a moment—just a moment—the rising floodwaters, the desperate crowd, the stern Warden with his ledger, all of it recedes. There's only the bell and the weight of years spent chasing its whisper through drowned temples and ruined archives. After all this time, is it finally calling to him, or is something in the marshland speaking in its voice?)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Warden Coss, that water's running too fast, and that sound—that's not a chapel bell. We need to get these families across, not hold them here while the marsh decides what it wants.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow studies the water level against the landing markers, his weathered face grim. He turns sharply toward the Warden, ears still tracking that wrong bell-sound from the reeds. His body language shifts into something more urgent—less disgraced guard, more someone who's held a line against worse things.)

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The taxes—yes, I know, Coss. But those families don't have time for your ledger, and neither do I. Let me ring them home, and I swear I'll settle what I owe you.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Coss's torch wavers as the three of you crowd him at once — Petra's plea, Anselm's strange certainty about the bell, Yarrow's blunt read of the rising water. He looks past you at the swelling black line already lapping the third step, then down at his ledger, and something in him breaks. 'Fine — fine!' He drags the chain back with a curse, waving the shivering families through ahead of you, torchlight jumping across wet faces as they stumble onto the causeway stones. But he grabs Petra's wrist as she passes, hard enough to make her flinch. 'Back-taxes, Petra. I'm writing it in the book tonight, in front of God and the toll-house, and you're paying every copper or I burn your father's name off the tollgate ledger myself.' The bell-sound drifts on, thin and wrong, past the reeds — and both Petra and Anselm feel it, unmistakably, listening back.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The causeway stones vanish under black water a hundred yards ahead of you — the flood has beaten you to it, chains and all. There's no going around; the only landmark left in the grey murk is the temple's belltower, a dark finger jutting above the waterline far off to the north. Petra swears under her breath, recognizing the shape of it even from here — she's heard those bells before, in dreams she didn't ask for. You'll have to swim, punt, or wade the rest of the way, trusting that stone tower to guide you true while the water climbs around your knees.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: That's Saint Orrin's tower—the bells are calling us left, toward the shallows.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra's breath catches as she recognizes the bell-tower even through the downpour—she's heard those bells before, in dreams she didn't ask for. The swarm-song threads through the rain, singing a path only she can perceive. She wades in slowly, testing each step, reading the current's pull and the gravel's grip beneath her feet, feeling where the causeway rises in its ancient ridge. Her hand rises, pointing left toward darker water where the stones still break the surface.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: These roads are mine — I grew up running them when they were dry. Follow close and keep your heads up; the currents know where they're going, and so do I.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm strips away his heavier layers and wades into the flood ahead of the others, his body moving with the confidence of a man returning to a half-drowned home. His fingers trail over submerged stones only he remembers. Each step finds the old mill-race beds that still hold high ground—the carved channels that once fed the mills of Hollowmoot, now highways through the black water. He reads the temperature shifts in the current the way other men read maps.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: The water's running north by northwest—we follow the shallow line past those willows. The temple's on high ground; we'll make it before the water climbs too high. Stay close to me.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow wades into the water and studies the current, reading how the floodwaters have shifted and moved. He traces a path along the willow trees toward the temple belltower, using his intimate knowledge of the Sallowmere's waterways to guide the group forward safely. He commands them to follow his lead, his hand steady on Brack's neck.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — overcome with Notice: dice 0 0 0 0 → Great (+4) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm — create advantage with Lore: dice + 0 0 0 → Superb (+5) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's outstretched hand finds true — the causeway's buried ridge holds firm underfoot exactly where she pointed, and the party edges left into darker water without a single misstep swallowing them. Behind her, Anselm cuts an even surer line: his fingers keep finding the old mill-race stones, and soon he's not just leading but reading the whole submerged road ahead, calling back depth and footing before anyone's boot even touches it — the group falls into his rhythm, Following the Drowned Mill-Roads now, trusting his instinct over the murk. Yarrow keeps pace at the rear with Brack pressed to his side, the hound's ears flat and swiveling, though nothing yet has set him growling. The belltower looms larger through the rain, but so does the sound beneath the sound of the storm — a low, wordless humming that seems to rise with the water itself.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The bells are singing with the water—they're calling us left, toward the high ground.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra closes her eyes and tilts her head back into the rain, reaching past the storm's roar for the swarm-song beneath. She uses the same senses that read weather and water to parse the humming rising with the floods—separating the bells' song from the chaos, feeling where the drowned paths twist, what the bells are singing. The water and the bells speak in the same wordless language, and she's learning to translate it.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: The bell-tongue still has a voice, even underwater. That's not the storm—that's the temple answering something in the flood. We need to know what's calling before we wade straight into it.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm raises a fist, halting the party's forward motion. He tilts his head, listening past the storm's roar to that low humming that pulses with the rising water. His fingers trail through the current, feeling for the rhythm. The ancient liturgies of Saint Orrin surface in his mind—not as words but as resonance, as the way sanctified stone remembers its own bells. The temple isn't just standing drowned. It's singing.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Moving steady. That sound is pulling from the north.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock wades forward into the flood with steady purpose, her strong frame moving through the current without strain. She keeps her focus split between the solid ground beneath her feet and the strange humming that rises with the water, her experienced senses alert.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: The water's singing something that doesn't belong here. Move faster toward that temple—whatever's singing will know we're coming soon enough.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow slows his pace, his grip tightening on Brack's neck as the hound's hackles rise beneath his palm. He tilts his head, reading the strange humming not just with his ears but with the whole length of his body, feeling it pulse up through the water at his knees like a pulse that shouldn't be there. Brack presses harder against his leg, ears flattened flat. Yarrow's jaw sets—this is no storm-sound, no simple flood-rush.)

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: No—no, that's my name, that's *my* name in the song—

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — overcome with Notice: dice - 0 + + → Superb (+5) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm — create advantage with Lore: dice - 0 - +, invoking Following the Drowned Mill-Roads [A-1.2.1] → Superb (+5) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The song coils around Petra's own name and for one long breath she goes rigid in the current, water climbing past her knees while the humming pulls at something in her chest she can't name — Freezes When the Song Calls Her Name, and it very nearly costs her the ford. But she claws the moment back, snapping her focus onto the shape of the water itself, and what she reads is uncanny: the flood isn't random here, it's answering the bells, rising and easing in time with that drowned hymn. Anselm's halted stillness pays off just as hard — the liturgy surfacing in his memory isn't ornament, it's instruction, and he can now read Saint Orrin's ritual resonance in the humming itself, a thread the whole party can follow straight to the tower without groping blind. Caddock pushes on through the current, steady and watchful, while Yarrow feels Brack's hackles rise harder with every yard closer — the hound knows something's wrong up ahead, even if it isn't barking yet. Through the rain, the belltower is close now, black stone rising dry above water that shouldn't still be climbing this fast.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The temple is still singing because it's waiting—it's been waiting for someone to answer the bells. That's why we're here. That's why I can hear it calling my name.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra wades deeper into the water toward the belltower, her breath coming fast as the swarm-song threads through the rain and storm. She reaches past her fear of hearing her own name in that humming and listens to what the bells are actually singing—not a lure into the dark, but a summons. The ritual resonance that Anselm sensed surfaces in her awareness too, but clearer: Saint Orrin's bells have been ringing this prayer into the flood for longer than anyone remembers, waiting for someone who could answer. Waiting for her. She feels the full weight of that purpose settle into her bones, steady as the pull of the tide.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: The bells remember their liturgy. The temple is answering something in the water—but the stones themselves are still dry above. That's where the Bell-Tongue waits. Follow my lead, stay close, move fast.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm turns toward the belltower and begins wading forward with renewed purpose, his body cutting through the current with the confidence of a man who knows both the old mill-roads beneath the water and the ritual heartbeat of the stones themselves. He reads the humming like a map written in faith and drowning stone, the liturgy of Saint Orrin becoming his compass.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Brack knows. Hold tight and let me take point—whatever's ahead, I'll find it before it finds us.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow's grip tightens on Brack's collar as the hound's muscles coil beneath his wet fur, a low thrumming growl rising in his chest. He turns to face his companions with the sharp, focused intensity of a man who has learned to read danger in water and weathering. His free hand settles on the knife at his belt as he shifts forward, placing himself between the group and the darkness ahead—the militia guard who still holds the line, drawing on years of watching the marshland's margins for threats. He reads the water's every ripple and shift, already hunting for the first sign of what Brack has already sensed.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — create advantage with Notice: dice - - 0 0 → Fair (+2) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's insight carries them the last stretch — the flood is *answering* the bells, not random at all, and once she reads that rhythm the crossing stops feeling like a fight against the water and starts feeling like a path someone left for them. Anselm strides ahead with the liturgy alive in his mind, calling out footing before anyone's boot finds it, and Caddock and Yarrow close the line behind him with Brack rigid but silent at Yarrow's side, hackles up but not yet howling. The belltower rises out of the murk at last — genuinely dry stone above a waterline that keeps climbing everywhere else — and the party hauls itself up out of the flood onto its worn steps, soaked, shaking, but whole. Below and around you the humming doesn't stop; if anything it's louder here, close enough now that it isn't just a song in the water anymore, it's a sound with a source, and that source is somewhere above you in the tower itself. Petra's hand is still trembling from hearing her own name in it, but she's first up the steps, already listening for what comes next.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: That Warden at the gate—scared, angry, wanting someone to swear they'd bring back answers. I gave my word. A promise made in anger binds just as tight, and I can't shake it.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow accepts the compel on 'Cursed to Keep Every Promise Made'.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The belltower rises black and dripping ahead, its bell-song threading through the rain. A skiff scrapes stone behind you, and there's Coss, half-frozen, ledger long since ruined, hauling himself onto the temple steps. 'Friend,' he calls out to Yarrow, still using the old word out of habit even now, disgraced or not — Wardens don't drop the habit easy. He says Yarrow promised him answers, and he won't leave without them. Water laps at the nave's broken doors, and somewhere above, out of sight, the bell keeps calling.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Coss, come on—we need higher ground. The bell's calling, and if the Warden at the gate sent you for answers, they're up in that tower, not down here drowning.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra grabs Coss's sodden sleeve and pulls him toward the temple steps, her ear already tracking the bell's rhythm. It's different now—urgent, weaving a pattern she knows intimately from years watching the bell-ringer at Ashwater. She glances back at Yarrow and the others, then upward at the belltower's dark silhouette, water dripping from the bell-frame. The swarm-song coils around her spine, not quite in words, but in shapes and weights that tell her the answers they need are up there, not out here in the rising dark.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: The bell pulled you here too, didn't it? Wardens don't break oath just for duty—something in that song has teeth.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm's gaze lifts toward the belltower where the bell still calls, then shifts to Coss, studying him with an exorcist's wariness. He doesn't move to help the half-frozen Warden up the temple steps, but he doesn't step back either—watching, assessing, as if checking for marks or signs the water and bell might have left on him.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Your word holds me, friend, same as mine holds you. But I need to know what answers settle this—what do you actually need me to bring back? Because I can't leave Coss shivering on these steps, and I won't break faith with you. So tell me true: what will it take?

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow reaches down and hauls Coss up the temple steps, steadying him against the stone. Water streams from the Warden's clothes. Yarrow meets his eyes, and there's no disgrace in his face now—just the weight of what he swore. He grips Coss's shoulder once, hard, the way soldiers do.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Coss's teeth chatter so hard the words come out broken. "The Warden captain—she's got kin gone up this water. Half a dozen crossed to pray at low tide and never came back down. She said find out if the bell's callin' the living or just... callin'." He grips the temple's broken doorframe, staring past all of you into the black nave where the water laps the second row of pews. "That's the answer I need, Yarrow. Not for me. For her." Behind him the swarm-song shifts key, weaving up through the flooded stone toward the belltower — and for a moment even Anselm's practiced ear catches something in it that isn't just noise. It's counting. Above the waterline, dry stone steps spiral up into the dark, and the bell keeps calling.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The bell's ringing a message, not a scream. I can read it if I get close enough—the Warden captain needs to know if it's calling them down or calling them home.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra doesn't wait for debate. She's already moving toward the spiral stairs, water streaming from her sleeves as she takes the steps two at a time, her ear tilted upward toward the belltower. The swarm-song coils around her spine like a rope she's learned to trust, and she follows it as the stone carries her higher, away from the flood and closer to the bell's true voice. She's spent years listening to bell-ringers, learning how each note carries meaning in the old marshland tongue—the Order's bell-lore she stole sings in her bones now, patterns burned into memory despite the price on her head. The bell above isn't ringing in panic; it's counting something deliberate, a rhythm that speaks beneath the rain and the water-song. She climbs toward it, determined to know what it's calling before the flood swallows the answer.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: It's counting. That's the old bell-rite—a call or a ward. I need to reach that bell and read what's being said.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm moves toward the spiral stairs with sharp purpose, already pulling up fragments of the old Saint Orrin liturgy in his mind. His ear tracks the counting pattern as he climbs, fingers trailing the temple stone for inscriptions, searching for any mark that might guide his understanding of what—or who—the bell is calling.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: The bell's counting something. The captain's kin—the answers they need are up there. I promised, and I keep my word.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow grips the stone railing and steps onto the spiral stairs, his eyes tracking the bell's rhythm. He reads the pattern like water-flow, each toll and silence mapping something toward the source of that counting. Moving carefully to avoid betraying his presence in the echoing tower, he climbs toward the answers Coss needs.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The stairs spiral up out of the rain's reach, and one by one you breach the belfry — dry stone, dry air, the first dry ground any of you have stood on in days. The bell itself hangs enormous and green with age, and it isn't swinging. Petra reaches it first and presses her palm flat to the bronze, feeling the counting pattern shiver up through her bones rather than her ears: it's the Order's old ward-count, the one rung to call scattered pilgrims *home* to consecrated ground — but someone has looped it, over and over, stripped of the verses that would ever let it stop. Anselm finds the proof scratched into the stone at the bell's foot: fresh chisel-marks gouging out the closing lines of the rite, deliberate and recent. Yarrow, closest to the stair, spots what the other two nearly climbed past — a coil of rope lashed to the clapper, feeding down through a gap in the floor into the flooded nave below, where something below the black water is pulling it, slow and patient, in perfect rhythm. Coss stares up at the bell like a man seeing a ghost. 'Then it's not calling them home,' he says, voice cracking. 'It's calling them *down*.' Whatever answer you carry back to the Warden captain, it isn't the one that lets her sleep.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: "No, no, no—" I gasp, feeling the song wrap around my own name and tighten.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra accepts the compel on 'Vow to Ring Everyone Home'.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's hand stays locked to the bronze, her name still coiling through the swarm-song — and it's in that frozen breath that she hears it: a second voice threading under the bell-tone, thin and human, humming the same pattern back. Not the bell ringing itself, then. Someone is up here with you, tucked in the belfry's shadow past the bell's black curve, matching the song note for note like a prayer they can't stop saying. Anselm's torch swings toward the sound and catches a huddled shape — soaked robes, hollow eyes, swaying in time with the bronze. One of the captain's kin, maybe, still breathing, still humming, not yet gone to whatever the song is calling them toward.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Hold on! I know the patterns—come back! What's your name?

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra tears her palm from the bell bronze and crosses the belfry toward the hunched figure, her voice rising to cut across their drone. She weaves between the notes she knows by heart from Saint Orrin's patterns, trying to pull them back with something human and graspable—a name, a voice, a way out of the song that's trying to drown them.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: In the name of Saint Orrin, I break this song's hold on you. You are not hive—you are your own soul.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps forward, torch held high, and begins reciting the old exorcism rite of Saint Orrin—the one he's spent years learning, the one that names the hive as foreign and severed from grace. His voice cuts through the belfry steady and certain, each word a liturgical spoke meant to pry open what the swarm-song has locked shut in this poor soul's mind.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I'm here. You're here too.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock approaches the swaying figure with quiet purpose, recognizing the signs of someone caught in a song they can't stop answering. She moves slow and steady, her hands open at her sides. This is the walk of a midwife—deliberate, calm, focused on keeping someone present in their own body.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: You're not lost yet—come back to us!

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow strides toward the humming pilgrim without hesitation, his boots splashing through the water on the belfry floor. He grabs their shoulders firmly, trying to break through the song's hold with his presence and will.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Not now. This soul comes first—Vex's whistle can wait.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm refuses the compel on 'Favor of Blackwater Lieutenant Vex'.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's voice finds the exact gap in the song — she matches the pilgrim's pattern note for note, then *breaks* it, sliding in a name-shaped silence where the swarm-tone should be. The humming stutters, catches, and the figure's head snaps up, eyes suddenly wet and human and terrified. In the same breath Anselm's rite lands clean: the old words of severance ring out over the bronze bell like a second, truer tone, and whatever thread the hive had sunk into this soul visibly slackens, the robed figure's shoulders sagging as if a hook has been pulled from behind the sternum. Yarrow reaches them a heartbeat later, hands closing on trembling shoulders — his grip holds, but the pilgrim flinches hard at the contact, the song still guttering weakly in their throat even as their eyes clear, some last thread of it clinging on despite everything. Caddock is there to catch them as their knees buckle, murmuring the same steady words she'd use for a birth gone wrong, and between the four of you the pilgrim comes back — gasping, sobbing, alive, and unmistakably *themself* again. They cling to Caddock's sleeve and choke out a name — not their own, but the captain's: "She said find them... she said the bell would call them home, but I heard my mother's voice in it, not God's." The bell above you all falls silent for the first time since you climbed the stair, and in the hush you can hear, faint and far off, the flood still rising against the temple's drowned nave below.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: This is Mory. I delivered her son Kel three winters before the Wardens burned us out. The night they came with torches, I told her: "Your boy lives. I'll see it done, or die swearing it."

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I hear those words again and something in me breaks like kindling. "Then I'm going after him. If the Wardens won't, I will—and every Warden who said it was for the greater good will know exactly what that cost."

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock accepts the compel on 'Last of Marrowreed Village'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: A gaunt, soot-scarred woman claws her way up the belfry stairs — one of the Marrowreed survivors Caddock knows by name, someone he thought had stayed safe behind in Hollowmoot. begs the party to go to the reed-choked shallows south of the temple, where innocent-looking mats of woven reed hide the sucking black mire beneath, because her son followed the swarm-song into the belltower.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Mory grips the belfry rail with both hands, soot-scarred knuckles white against green bronze, and doesn't let go of Caddock's sleeve even after she's said it. "The reeds south of here — Kel went in after the song, three days back, maybe more. Mats of reed lie flat on the water like solid ground, Caddock, you know that stretch, you know what's under it." Behind her the bell's low hum hasn't stopped, and rain sheets off the belfry's dry stone into the black water below, where somewhere south the mire waits under its deceptive green skin. Coss shifts by the stairwell, torn between the Warden captain's orders and the sight of a mother begging a midwife she once might have arrested. The path south means trusting Caddock's old ground-sense against ground that swallows the unwary whole — and every minute spent deciding is a minute the swarm-song has Kel to itself.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I've been reading water and ground since I could walk, Mory—I can navigate the mire. I hear your son in the song, still listening back. I'm going to bring him home.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra turns from the bell to face Mory, her palm still vibrating with the bronze's rhythm. She's heard the swarm-song her whole life—knows the difference between singing that calls and the silence of someone listening back. Kel's in there, answering. She steps toward Mory with absolute certainty, her movement decisive.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: How long has Kel been in the reeds? And when the song took him—was he walking into it willing, or did it pull? There's a difference, and I need to know which one I'm cutting.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm turns to face Mory, eyes sharp with the clarity of someone who has learned to read possession and compulsion. He wants to understand whether Kel walked into the mire or was dragged by the song—it changes everything about how to retrieve him. He glances back at the still-humming bell, then toward the southern stairs.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I know that ground. I've walked it before the burning. Hold here—I'll bring him back.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock grips Mory's soot-scarred hand back, meets her eyes for one steady moment, then pulls free and heads for the spiral stairs without hesitation. Her jaw is set and her breathing steady—the midwife's calm, the kind that doesn't break even when the water is rising.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: The mire will get worse the longer we stand here talking. I know that ground—my kin mapped every ford and false-step in these shallows. We go now, we go careful, and we go together. I'll read the water.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow steps to the belfry edge, eyes already tracking the rain-dark water southward toward the reed beds. He's quiet for a moment, reading the flow like he reads faces—feeling the current's pull, the weight of what's underneath. Then he turns back to the group, jaw set hard. He crosses to Mory and puts a weathered hand on her shoulder, brief and solid. He moves for the stairs without waiting for agreement.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The party goes down through the belfry's dry throat and back into the rain, Caddock in the lead with a midwife's steady stride across ground she buried a hundred memories in. True to its tags, the Sucking Mire hides beneath reed mats that look solid as any road — and for one gut-lurching moment the black water swallows Caddock to the waist before Yarrow's hand and his weir-keeper's eye for the current find the firm line along old pilings just in time to haul her clear, soaked and furious but upright. Petra pushes ahead once the ground steadies, her whole body tuned to the bell-pattern, and she's the one who finds him: a boy no older than ten, chest-deep in reed and mud, humming the swarm-song back to the water with wide, unblinking eyes, his skin already showing the first grey bloom of the hive along one arm. Anselm reaches him a breath later and reads it plain — Kel didn't walk in willing, the song pulled him, and it hasn't finished pulling. Between the four of you — Yarrow's grip, Anselm's counter-rite murmured low and steady, Petra breaking the pattern the way she broke it for the pilgrim above — you drag Kel free of the mire's hold and the song's both, and Mory's cry when she sees him carried up the belfry stairs, alive, answers every question the reeds tried to ask. He is not whole — the grey on his arm says the hive has him in some measure now — but he is breathing, and he is hers.
